Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' appears trauma-incongruent unless there is a clear secondary road-traffic component; nothing elsewhere in the profile supports a vehicle-related trauma theme, so this trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the assault-focused profile.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is largely centered on interpersonal/ambient danger after assault (silence, unexpected sounds), but 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' suggests a broader environmental danger pattern. This is not inherently implausible, but combined with the car-crash trigger it contributes to a mismatched threat context that is not otherwise represented in memory or appraisals.

vignette: Thanya Vance was five years into her surgical practice when the Tuesday night commute through the hospital's lower parking garage turned violent. She had been walking alone, her stethoscope still around her neck, when a man stepped from behind a concrete pillar and pinned her wrists to her sides, his forearm pressing against her throat. In the flickering fluorescent light, she had watched a jagged scar pull at his left cheek, caught the sharp, acrid scent of stale tobacco and damp asphalt, and later seen the blue and red flash of police lights cutting through the garage haze as officers arrived. She had come to believe that the ordinary rules of the world had fractured in those seconds. The sight of her own wrists, still pale and marked, made her avoid mirrors. She found herself tracking other people's throats and forearms in crowded hallways, her gaze snagging on the exact shapes that had been confined. Even the sight of a police cruiser parked outside the clinic or an officer speaking at the end of the hallway sent her toward the exit. When a man with a similar scar line appeared in the pharmacy queue, she crossed the street without a second thought. What frightened her most was the way the memory refused to settle; she was certain that recalling it would unleash the same suffocating terror, so she had long ago stopped trying to picture it. Over the following months, the hospital itself became a landscape of vigilance. During morning rounds on the surgical floor, the unusual silence between patient checks made her grip the supply cart until her knuckles whitened, convinced that something dangerous was about to materialize. When a code blue alarm blared or a gasket door slammed, her shoulders shot up, her breath catching before she could steady it. In the humid summer months, she began wearing oversized cardigans and high-collared blouses over her scrubs, believing that drawing attention to her face or frame would only invite another violation. She avoided anything that reminded her of the man in the garage, rerouting her drives and checking the scent of passing colleagues before entering patient rooms. She had lost her faith in people, in the rhythm of ordinary days, and in any higher power that might have watched over the lower garage. She had come to believe that her understanding of how the world worked had been completely destroyed. To quiet the relentless background noise, she would drive to the casino on her days off, buying tickets and watching cards flip, chasing a sudden rush that briefly drowned out the static in her head. Her husband noticed the distance. He had learned not to question why she canceled their Friday dinners when a familiar face appeared in the clinic lobby or why she flinched when he reached for her arm in bed. She told him she was simply exhausted, but the truth lived in the quiet space between them. Her attending physician had finally urged her to seek specialty support after noticing her avoiding in-person patient encounters and taking unnecessary early shifts to bypass the garage entirely. Thanya came to the consultation hoping to find a way to reclaim her practice and her marriage, terrified that the world would always feel like a place where silence signaled impending violence and strangers carried hidden threats. She was most afraid of never feeling safe again, but she hoped, against every shattered belief, to learn how to carry the past without letting it dictate her days.
